title: Is France heading for a new 1789?
gist: The authors argue France's fiscal position (debt 115.6% of GDP, deficit 5.1%, a hung Assembly) parallels the late Ancien Regime, where a budget crisis became a crisis of legitimacy; they stop short of predicting revolution but flag the 2027 elections as the test.

insights.claim: France ended 2025 with public debt at 115.6% of GDP and a deficit of 5.1%; Moody's downgraded French debt in December 2024 and by October 2026 the rating carried a negative outlook, with ten-year borrowing costs approaching 5%.
insights.speaker: Basile Marin and Léo Marin
insights.so_what: Sovereign credit and OAT spread risk stays elevated; watch further rating actions and OAT-Bund spreads.
insights.locator: Behind the urban disorder in France

insights.claim: Since the 2024 fragmentation of the National Assembly no French government has a dependable majority for an ordinary budget; the 2026 budget was forced through with Article 49.3, and the 2027 presidential election makes adjustment both urgent and politically explosive.
insights.speaker: Basile Marin and Léo Marin
insights.so_what: Fiscal consolidation is unlikely before 2027; budget votes are recurring event risk for French bonds.
insights.locator: Since the fragmentation of the National Assembly in 2024

insights.claim: With levies already at 43.6% of GDP, room to raise revenue in France is narrow, so any substantial adjustment depends on drastic spending cuts; interest payments reached about EUR 64.7bn in 2025, up 11.2% from 2024.
insights.speaker: Basile Marin and Léo Marin
insights.so_what: Debt service is a rising, non-discretionary claim on the budget; tax-led fixes are largely exhausted.
insights.locator: In 2025, with levies already amounting to 43.6 per cent of GDP

insights.claim: In 2025 transfer spending was 45% of French public expenditure and 56% of French people received more than they contribute; 72% favour fixing finances via spending cuts over tax rises, but only 29% back a pension freeze and 21% a doubling of medical deductibles.
insights.speaker: Basile Marin and Léo Marin
insights.so_what: Public support for cuts is abstract; concrete measures lack majorities, so reform slippage is the base case.
insights.locator: In 2025, 45 per cent of public expenditure consisted of transfer spending

insights.claim: The pension-freeze divide is generational: 84% of retirees oppose it while nearly half of 18-to-34-year-olds support one, making the allocation of fiscal pain a polarising political fault line.
insights.speaker: Basile Marin and Léo Marin
insights.so_what: Reforming social spending risks a major political crisis; not reforming guarantees a harsher later adjustment.

insights.claim: The key parallel with 1789 is not that revolution is inevitable but that a fiscal crisis can quickly turn into a crisis of political legitimacy, as the 1788 Treasury payment suspension and the Estates-General turned a budget problem into a fight over who may allocate national resources.
insights.speaker: Basile Marin and Léo Marin
insights.so_what: Treat French fiscal gridlock as a regime-stability risk, not just a spread story.
insights.quote: a fiscal crisis can quickly transform into a crisis of political legitimacy
insights.locator: The parallel with the waning years of the Ancien Régime

insights.claim: Ancien Regime debt (56-70% of GDP) was lower than France's 115.6% today, but its 5-6% interest rate was far higher than the roughly 3.9% ten-year OAT in 2025; more than half the royal budget went to debt service and markets punished the absence of effective reform.
insights.speaker: Basile Marin and Léo Marin
insights.so_what: Today's lower rates are the main buffer; a rate shock would make the analogy bite much harder.
insights.locator: The debt of the Ancien Régime, at 56-70 per cent of GDP

insights.claim: The 1785 deficit was about 3% of GDP (about 20% of revenue) against 5% of GDP in 2025 (about 9.8% of revenue), because the modern French state takes about 52% of GDP in revenue versus about 15% then.
insights.speaker: Basile Marin and Léo Marin
insights.so_what: France has more fiscal capacity than the monarchy had, but the headroom is largely used.
insights.locator: In 1785, the public deficit was approximately three per cent

insights.claim: Elites in both eras held an illusion of immutable order: Louis XVI's contemporaries believed until the last moment that the system could endure unchanged, so calm markets and complacent elites are weak evidence of stability.
insights.speaker: Basile Marin and Léo Marin
insights.so_what: Do not extrapolate France's current stability; tail-risk pricing may be too thin.
insights.locator: It is impossible to predict whether the point of no return

themes.theme: A society of orders and political blocs

insights.claim: Modern France is split into three classes with distinct ideologies: a governing class favouring liberalism and European integration, a normative class favouring progressive egalitarianism, and a productive class (workers, farmers, small business) increasingly favouring protectionism.
insights.speaker: Basile Marin and Léo Marin
insights.so_what: Useful map for forecasting coalition outcomes; the productive-class bloc feeds the National Rally.
insights.locator: Modern French society can, schematically, be divided into three classes

insights.claim: High social reproduction and low mobility make contemporary France resemble a society of orders, and status strongly predicts voting: working-class voters have moved strongly to the National Rally while higher professionals stay centrist or liberal.
insights.speaker: Basile Marin and Léo Marin
insights.so_what: Class-based voting supports a durable populist-right base entering 2027.
insights.locator: With high levels of social reproduction and low social mobility

insights.claim: The authors frame the modern conflict as universalism versus Counter-Enlightenment organicism, and say a 21st-century 'Counter-Revolution' could be as fundamental a rupture as 1789.
insights.speaker: Basile Marin and Léo Marin
insights.so_what: Raises the stakes of 2027: outcomes could shift France's institutional and EU posture, not just policy.
insights.locator: In fact, the modern conflict still revolves around the same fundamental questions

insights.claim: The 2027 elections will be a test of French institutions, especially if they yield a National Assembly without a stable majority or if parties do not respect the outcome.
insights.speaker: Basile Marin and Léo Marin
insights.so_what: Hung-parliament and contested-result scenarios are the French political tail risks to watch.
insights.locator: The 2027 elections will probably constitute another test
